current_episode.title: How to Reach the Unreachable Voter

guest.bio_context: Danielle Butterfield joined the Priorities USA team in 2017 fresh off the Hillary Clinton campaign, initially serving as Digital Director. She negotiated to build an in-house team to focus purely on innovation rather than working with outside consultants driven by profit margins. Under her leadership, Priorities USA transitioned from a traditional presidential super PAC into an organization anchored in digital research, infrastructure, and innovation across election cycles.

pending_qa.q: Did Democrats close the digital spending gap between 2016 and 2024?
pending_qa.r: In 2024, Democrats actually outspent Republicans two to one on digital, so it is no longer a numbers problem. According to Butterfield, the real issue is several layers deeper: Democrats are still running digital programs that mirror television strategy, which makes the problem much harder to diagnose and solve.

pending_qa.q: Why is running TV ads on YouTube a failed strategy for Democratic campaigns?
pending_qa.r: Butterfield states that nine out of the ten top YouTube ads in 2024 were simply 30-second TV ads repurposed for the platform. She argues this is 'quite literally lighting money on fire' because YouTube audiences have fragmented attention spans, consume content in vastly different ways — podcasts, music, gaming, clips — and the platform should not be treated as a broadcast channel.

pending_qa.q: What role do political consultants play in perpetuating outdated digital strategies?
pending_qa.r: Butterfield points to the consultant-driven nature of campaign decision-making as a core obstacle: producing 20 tailored digital ads instead of one TV spot eats into profit margins for consultants, creating a structural tension between paying bills and winning elections. This is partly why Priorities USA built an in-house team insulated from those incentives.

pending_qa.q: What did Priorities USA's post-2024 research reveal about YouTube consumption and vote behavior?
pending_qa.r: Priorities USA found that YouTube consumption was more predictive of vote choice and vote swing from 2020 to 2024 than age, demographic, or geographic indicators. Specifically, men watching more than three hours of YouTube per day showed some of the highest vote swing toward Trump of any cross-tab examined, and the pattern held for podcast listeners and women as well.

pending_qa.q: How does Priorities USA study the media habits of less politically engaged voters?
pending_qa.r: Priorities USA runs an always-on survey operation where participants are paid to send screenshots of their screen-time apps, which are then validated against self-reported data to track shifts in platform usage, subscriptions, and new app adoption. They complement this with quarterly or monthly deep dives on specific topics — such as audio consumption — and acquire third-party behavioral data including search histories.

pending_qa.q: What was the methodology and scale of the Priorities USA search behavior study?
pending_qa.r: The study analyzed approximately six million searches from opted-in users who shared their behavioral data with a third-party provider. It covered two time periods — late 2024 and a portion of 2025 — and included data from Google, Gemini, ChatGPT, YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, and Facebook. The team used AI extensively to process and analyze the large dataset.

pending_qa.q: How has the definition of 'search' changed and what platforms are now part of the search landscape?
pending_qa.r: Butterfield describes Google as still holding predominant market share and making the majority of its revenue from search. However, as people spend more time online, they are using multiple platforms simultaneously rather than choosing between them, and distinct search behaviors are emerging across Google, TikTok, Instagram, and AI platforms like ChatGPT and Gemini.

pending_qa.q: What is the Priorities USA $30 million campaign targeting in 2025–2026?
pending_qa.r: Priorities USA has already launched a $30 million campaign aimed at defining 2028 Republican figures such as J.D. Vance and Marco Rubio during the current 2026 election cycle. The strategy reflects their view that the 2028 presidential race will effectively begin the day after the 2026 midterms.
